records.source: Λέγω δέ, ἐφ’ ὅσον χρόνον ὁ κληρονόμος νήπιός ἐστιν, οὐδὲν διαφέρει δούλου κύριος πάντων ὤν, ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπους ἐστὶ καὶ οἰκονόμους ἄχρι τῆς προθεσμίας τοῦ πατρός.
records.gloss: I say now, for as much time [as] the heir a child is, nothing he differs from a slave, lord of all being, \v 2 but under guardians he is and managers until the set-beforehand [time] of the father.
pieces: Here is what I mean. While the heir is still a child, his position is no better than a slave's, even though he is master of everything.
Guardians and managers have charge of him until the date his father has set.

L.1: Now I say, for as long a time as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, though he is lord of all,
L.2: but he is under guardians and managers until the time set beforehand by the father.

R.1: Think of it like this. A child who will inherit everything his father owns is no better off than a slave while he is still young, even though it all belongs to him.
R.2: Other people are put in charge of him and of his property until the time his father has chosen.

decisions.choice: a child under age: a minor, not yet legally able to act for himself
decisions.reason: νήπιος can mean a baby, but here it stands against the grown heir who takes control of the estate. The point is legal standing, not age in years: until the set time the heir cannot manage what is his.

decisions.choice: though he is owner of everything: owner by right, not yet in practice
alternatives: he is already in control of the estate
decisions.reason: The participle is concessive. The estate already belongs to the heir, yet while he is under age he has no more say over it than a slave of the household.

decisions.choice: guardians and managers: those who had charge of a minor and of his property
decisions.reason: An ἐπίτροπος was a guardian appointed for a child, and an οἰκονόμος was a steward who ran property or a household. Greek and Roman law both made such arrangements for heirs who were under age. Paul uses the two words together for the people who had charge over the child and over what he would inherit.

decisions.choice: the date set in advance by the father
decisions.reason: προθεσμία is a time fixed beforehand. Paul's picture does not fit any one legal system exactly, and it does not say whether the father is living or dead. What matters for his argument is that the father decides when the heir comes of age, as God set the time in verse 4.

decisions.choice: managers
decisions.reason: "Steward" is now an uncommon word; "managers" says what these people did.

decisions.choice: a child who will inherit everything his father owns
decisions.reason: Readable explains what an heir is and repeats the estate so the picture is clear to a young reader.

decisions.choice: slave / a slave's
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it in Galatians 4–5: the slave who owns nothing is set against the heir who owns everything, and against the son and the freedom of 4:5-7.

records.heading: No longer slaves but heirs

records.source: οὕτως καὶ ἡμεῖς, ὅτε ἦμεν νήπιοι, ὑπὸ τὰ στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου ἤμεθα δεδουλωμένοι·
records.gloss: So also we, when we were children, under the elements of the world we were enslaved;
pieces: In the same way we too, when we were children, were held as slaves under the elemental forces of the world.

L.3: So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of the world.

R.3: It was the same for us. When we were like young children, we were slaves to the powers and rules that run this world.

decisions.choice: we: Paul and all believers, Jews and Gentiles alike, before Christ came
alternatives: we Jews, who lived under the law
decisions.reason: The "we" could be Paul and his fellow Jews, held under the law as a guardian (3:23-25). But in verses 8-9 Paul tells the Galatians, who were Gentiles, that taking up the law would be turning back to the same elemental things they served before. So the "we" most likely includes everyone, each under the form of slavery that belonged to life before Christ.

decisions.choice: the elemental forces of the world: the basic powers and principles thought to govern life in this world, and the religious rules bound up with them
alternatives: the elementary principles or ABCs of religion
elemental spirits: spiritual beings ruling the world
decisions.reason: στοιχεῖα means the basic parts of something: the letters of the alphabet, the elements (earth, water, air, fire) of which the world was thought to be made, or the ABCs of a subject (Hebrews 5:12). In the thinking of the time the elements were linked with the stars and with spiritual powers. Here Paul ties them to slavery, to beings that are not gods (verse 8), and to keeping days and months and seasons (verse 10). So the phrase may mean the elementary rules of religion, Jewish and pagan alike, or the powers thought to rule the world through them; for Paul's readers the two belonged together. Colossians 2:8 and 2:20 use the same phrase.

decisions.choice: we were held as slaves: a lasting condition, not a single event
decisions.reason: The verb is a past tense with a perfect participle: a settled state of slavery, which the coming of the Son ends (verses 4-5).

decisions.choice: the elements of the world (L); the elemental forces of the world (B); the powers and rules that run this world (R)
alternatives: the basic principles of the world
the elemental spirits of the world
decisions.reason: As in Colossians 2:8: Literal keeps the bare word, Balanced uses a phrase that keeps both senses of m2 open, and Readable names both.

decisions.choice: like young children
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that Paul is comparing believers to the heir under age in verse 1, not speaking of childhood.

decisions.choice: held as slaves / slaves
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery under the law or the elemental forces is set against freedom (Galatians 4–5). The slavery ends when the Son comes (m3).

records.source: ὅτε δὲ ἦλθεν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου, ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός, γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμον, ἵνα τοὺς ὑπὸ νόμον ἐξαγοράσῃ, ἵνα τὴν υἱοθεσίαν ἀπολάβωμεν.
records.gloss: But when came the fullness of the time, sent out the God the Son of him, having come to be from a woman, having come to be under law, \v 5 so that those under law he might redeem, so that the adoption we might receive.
pieces: But when the time God had set was complete, God sent out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son. He was born of a woman and born under the law,
to redeem those who lived under the law, so that we might be adopted as {{gender:children|sons}}.

L.4: But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son, born of a woman, born under [the] law,
L.5: so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} might redeem those under [the] law, so that we might receive the adoption as {{gender:children|sons}}.

R.4: But when the right time came, God sent {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son. He was born of a woman, and born under the law.
R.5: God sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to buy freedom for those who were under the law, so that God could adopt us as {{gender:children|sons}}.

decisions.choice: the fullness of the time: the moment God had set
alternatives: simply "when the time was right" in a general sense
decisions.reason: The phrase answers "the time set beforehand by the father" in verse 2. The time of slavery ran until the date God had fixed, and then it was complete.

decisions.choice: God sent out his Son from himself
alternatives: God commissioned a man for a task, as he sent the prophets
decisions.reason: ἐξαποστέλλω means to send someone out on a mission. Paul uses the same verb for the Spirit in verse 6. He speaks of the one sent as already God's Son when he was sent, and only then of his birth, which fits his teaching elsewhere that the Son was with God before he came (Philippians 2:6-7).

decisions.choice: born of a woman, born under the law: truly human, and a Jew under Moses' law
alternatives: a statement about the virgin birth
decisions.reason: γίνομαι means "to come to be" and is used of birth. "Born of a woman" was a common way of saying "a human being" (Job 14:1; Matthew 11:11). Paul is not discussing how Jesus was conceived; he is saying the Son shared the condition of those he came to free. "Under the law" means he lived as a Jew under Moses' law, the very place of those he redeems.

decisions.choice: redeem: buy out of slavery, set free at a price
alternatives: rescue, without the idea of a price
decisions.reason: ἐξαγοράζω is the verb of 3:13, where Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. It comes from the marketplace: buying someone out of another's ownership.

decisions.choice: adoption as sons: being made a son and heir by law
alternatives: adoption as children, without the idea of heirship
decisions.reason: υἱοθεσία is the legal word for adoption. In Roman law an adopted son received the full rights of a son born into the family, including the inheritance. In this family the inheritance and the standing went with sonship, and Paul gives that standing to every believer, women as much as men (3:28-29).

decisions.choice: adoption as {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: The word gives the standing of a son and heir (m5), which Paul gives to men and women alike. The inclusive default says who is adopted; the traditional setting keeps "sons", which shows the legal standing more plainly.

decisions.choice: the time God had set was complete (B); the right time came (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the sense of a time filled up to its set point; Readable says it plainly.

decisions.choice: God sent him to buy freedom for
decisions.reason: Readable starts a new sentence, so it repeats who sent the Son, and it explains "redeem" as buying someone's freedom (m4).

records.source: ὅτι δέ ἐστε υἱοί, ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν, κρᾶζον· Αββα ὁ πατήρ.
records.gloss: And because you are sons, sent out the God the Spirit of the Son of him into the hearts of us, crying, Abba, the Father.
pieces: And since you are {{gender:children|sons}}, God has sent out the Spirit of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son into our hearts, and the Spirit cries, "Abba, Father!"

L.6: And because you are {{gender:children|sons}}, God sent out the Spirit of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son into our hearts, crying, "Abba, Father!"

R.6: You are God's {{gender:children|sons}}, and because of that, God has put the Spirit of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Son in our hearts. The Spirit cries out to God, "Abba! Father!"

decisions.choice: because you are sons, God sent the Spirit
alternatives: to show that you are sons, God sent the Spirit
decisions.reason: ὅτι here most naturally gives the reason: God gives the Spirit to those who are already his sons. Some read it as "the proof that you are sons is that God sent the Spirit", which fits 3:2-5, where receiving the Spirit is the sign that they belong. Either way, having the Spirit and being God's sons go together.

decisions.choice: sons: the standing of a son and heir, given to all believers
decisions.reason: υἱός is the word for a son, and in a family it carried the standing of a son and heir: in this setting daughters did not usually inherit as sons did. Paul gives that full standing to every believer, and he has just said that in Christ there is neither male nor female (3:28-29), so women share it on the same terms as men.

decisions.choice: into our hearts: Paul moves from "you" to "us"
decisions.reason: Paul begins with "you are sons" and ends with "our hearts": he and the Galatians receive the same Spirit, Jew and Gentile alike.

decisions.choice: Abba: the Aramaic word for "father", followed by the Greek word
decisions.reason: Αββα is the Aramaic word a child used for a father, and the word Jesus used in his own prayer (Mark 14:36). The Greek churches kept the Aramaic word and added its translation, as Romans 8:15 also does. Believers address God the way the Son does.

decisions.choice: the Spirit cries out
alternatives: we cry out, moved by the Spirit
decisions.reason: The participle κρᾶζον agrees with the word for Spirit, so it is the Spirit who cries out in believers' hearts. In Romans 8:15 it is "we" who cry "Abba"; the two passages describe the same prayer from two sides.

decisions.choice: {{gender:children|sons}}
decisions.reason: As in verse 5: the inclusive default names everyone who has this standing, and the traditional setting keeps "sons".

decisions.choice: and the Spirit cries (B); the Spirit cries out to God (R)
decisions.reason: English needs the subject of the participle made clear (m5), and the Spirit is never "it".

records.source: ὥστε οὐκέτι εἶ δοῦλος ἀλλὰ υἱός· εἰ δὲ υἱός, καὶ κληρονόμος διὰ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: So no longer are you a slave but a son; and if a son, also an heir through God.
pieces: So you are no longer a slave but {{gender:a child|a son}}, and if you are {{gender:a child|a son}}, then you are also an heir, made so by God.

L.7: So you are no longer a slave but {{gender:a child|a son}}, and if {{gender:a child|a son}}, also an heir through God.

R.7: So you are not a slave anymore. You are God's {{gender:child|son}}. And since you are God's {{gender:child|son}}, God has made you an heir as well.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "an heir through God"
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ here. Many later ones read "an heir of God through Christ", and a few have other wordings. The SBLGNT follows early manuscripts with the short reading "through God", which copyists seem to have filled out because it is unusual. The meaning is the same: the inheritance is God's gift.

decisions.choice: you, singular: each believer in person
decisions.reason: Paul has spoken to the Galatians as a group; here he turns to each one individually. What is true of the church is true of every member.

decisions.choice: son: the standing of a son and heir, given to all believers
decisions.reason: υἱός is the word for a son, and in a family it carried the standing of a son and heir: in this setting daughters did not usually inherit as sons did. Paul gives that full standing to every believer, and he has just said that in Christ there is neither male nor female (3:28-29), so women share it on the same terms as men.

decisions.choice: heir: one who will receive what God promised Abraham
decisions.reason: κληρονόμος takes up the picture of verse 1 and the promise of 3:18 and 3:29. The inheritance is what God promised Abraham and his offspring, received now through the Spirit (3:14) and in full later.

decisions.choice: {{gender:a child|a son}}
decisions.reason: As in verses 5-6.

decisions.choice: made so by God (B); God has made you an heir (R)
decisions.reason: "Through God" means God is the one who makes them heirs; Balanced and Readable say so.

decisions.choice: slave
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free: here the slave is set against the son and heir.

records.source: Ἀλλὰ τότε μὲν οὐκ εἰδότες θεὸν ἐδουλεύσατε τοῖς φύσει μὴ οὖσι θεοῖς·
records.gloss: But then indeed not knowing God you were slaves to the [ones] by nature not being gods;
pieces: In the past you did not know God, and you were slaves to beings that are not gods by nature.

L.8: But at that time, not knowing God, you were slaves to those [that] by nature are not gods.

R.8: Before, when you did not know God, you were slaves to gods that are not really gods at all.

decisions.choice: at that time: the Galatians' pagan past
decisions.reason: Paul now speaks to the Galatians as former Gentile worshipers. "At that time" is set against "now" in verse 9.

decisions.choice: beings that by nature are not gods
alternatives: idols that are nothing at all
spiritual powers that are real but not divine
decisions.reason: Paul does not say whether these "gods" are nothing or are real powers falsely worshiped. Elsewhere he says an idol is nothing (1 Corinthians 8:4) but also that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons (1 Corinthians 10:19-20). Here his point is only that whatever they are, they are not gods by nature.

decisions.choice: you were slaves to them
decisions.reason: δουλεύω means to serve as a slave. It keeps the picture of slavery from verses 1-7: their former religion was a kind of bondage.

decisions.choice: beings (B); gods that are not really gods at all (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek article stands for whatever is worshiped. Balanced names them as beings; Readable repeats "gods" to make the contrast plain. Neither decides whether they are real powers (m2).

decisions.choice: slaves
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery under the law or the elemental forces is set against freedom (Galatians 4–5). The former religion of the Galatians was bondage (m3).

records.heading: Why turn back to slavery?

records.source: νῦν δὲ γνόντες θεόν, μᾶλλον δὲ γνωσθέντες ὑπὸ θεοῦ, πῶς ἐπιστρέφετε πάλιν ἐπὶ τὰ ἀσθενῆ καὶ πτωχὰ στοιχεῖα, οἷς πάλιν ἄνωθεν δουλεύειν θέλετε;
records.gloss: but now having known God, rather but having been known by God, how do you turn again to the weak and poor elements, to which again from above to be slaves you want?
pieces: But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you go back to those weak and worthless elemental forces and want to serve them as slaves once more?

L.9: But now, having come to know God, or rather having been known by God, how [is it that] you are turning back again to the weak and poor elements, to which you want to be enslaved all over again?

R.9: But now you know God. Even more, God knows you as {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own. So how can you turn back to those weak and useless powers and rules? Do you really want to be their slaves all over again?

decisions.choice: known by God: God has taken them as his own
alternatives: God has become aware of them
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures, God's "knowing" people means choosing them and making them his own (Amos 3:2; 1 Corinthians 8:3). Paul corrects himself: their knowing God is real, but it rests on God's first knowing them.

decisions.choice: the weak and poor elemental forces: the same "elements" as verse 3
decisions.reason: στοιχεῖον is the word of verse 3; see the note there. They are "weak" because they cannot set anyone free, and "poor" because they have nothing to give, unlike the inheritance of verse 7.

decisions.choice: turning back again: taking up the law would be a return to slavery
decisions.reason: The Galatians are being urged to keep the Jewish law, not to return to idols. Yet Paul calls it turning back "again". Living under the law as the way to belong to God would put them back under the same kind of bondage they knew as pagans, because both belong to the time before Christ.

decisions.choice: all over again: from the beginning once more
decisions.reason: πάλιν ἄνωθεν doubles the idea of "again": they would be going back to the very start.

decisions.choice: elements (L); elemental forces (B); powers and rules (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 3.

decisions.choice: worthless (B); useless (R)
decisions.reason: "Poor" here means having nothing to give; Balanced and Readable use a word that says that.

decisions.choice: God knows you as his own
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what being known by God means (m1).

decisions.choice: serve them as slaves / be their slaves
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery under the law or the elemental forces is set against freedom (Galatians 4–5). Turning back would be a return to slavery (m3).

records.source: ἡμέρας παρατηρεῖσθε καὶ μῆνας καὶ καιροὺς καὶ ἐνιαυτούς.
records.gloss: Days you observe and months and seasons and years.
pieces: You keep special days and months, seasons and years.

L.10: You are observing days and months and seasons and years.

R.10: You carefully keep special days and months and seasons and years.

decisions.choice: a statement: you are observing
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates this as a statement, and the Galatians had evidently begun to keep these times. It could also be read as an indignant question; the meaning is much the same.

decisions.choice: days, months, seasons and years: the sacred calendar
decisions.reason: Those troubling the Galatians were urging them to keep the Jewish calendar: sabbaths, new moons, festivals, and perhaps the sabbath years. Paul's general words would fit pagan calendars just as well, which is his point in verse 9: a religion tied to the turning of the heavens belongs to the old order.

decisions.choice: observe carefully
decisions.reason: παρατηρέω means to watch closely, here of keeping religious times with scrupulous care.

decisions.choice: special days
decisions.reason: The days are sacred days, not ordinary ones; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: φοβοῦμαι ὑμᾶς μή πως εἰκῇ κεκοπίακα εἰς ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: I fear for you lest somehow in vain I have labored for you.
pieces: I am afraid for you. I fear that the work I did for you may have been wasted.

L.11: I fear for you, that somehow I have labored for you in vain.

R.11: I am worried about you. I am afraid that all my hard work for you has been for nothing.

decisions.choice: a fear that the harm may already be done
decisions.reason: After a verb of fearing, the perfect tense says Paul fears something may already have happened: that his work among them has already come to nothing.

decisions.choice: labored: worked hard to the point of weariness
decisions.reason: κοπιάω is Paul's word for the hard work of his mission (1 Corinthians 15:10; Philippians 2:16).

records.source: Γίνεσθε ὡς ἐγώ, ὅτι κἀγὼ ὡς ὑμεῖς, ἀδελφοί, δέομαι ὑμῶν.
records.gloss: Become as I, because I also as you, brothers, I beg you.
pieces: Be as I am, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, I beg you, since I made myself as you were.

L.12: Become as I [am], because I also [became] as you [were], {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, I beg you.

R.12: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, please, be like me. After all, I became like you.

decisions.choice: become as I am, because I became as you were: free from the law
alternatives: become as I am, because I am as you are
decisions.reason: The verbs must be supplied. Paul, a Jew, lived like a Gentile among the Galatians, not relying on the law (2:14; 1 Corinthians 9:21). He now asks them to be like him, free from the law, and not to take it up. The second clause can also be read "I am as you are", with the same point.

decisions.choice: "brothers, I beg you" ends the appeal
alternatives: it begins what follows: "Brothers, I beg you: you did me no wrong"
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT closes the sentence after "I beg you". The words may instead introduce what comes next; the warmth of the appeal is the same either way.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is speaking to the whole church; the inclusive default spells that out.

decisions.choice: I am (L, B); I became (L, R), I made myself (B)
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves out both verbs (m1).

records.heading: Paul pleads with the Galatians

records.source: οὐδέν με ἠδικήσατε·
records.gloss: Nothing me you wronged;
pieces: You did me no wrong.

L.12: In nothing did you wrong me.

R.12: When I was with you, you did nothing wrong to me.

decisions.choice: you did me no wrong: on my first visit
alternatives: you have done me no wrong now
decisions.reason: The past tense looks back to his first stay with them, described in verses 13-14. Paul is not nursing a personal grievance; the issue between them is the gospel.

decisions.choice: When I was with you
decisions.reason: Readable says which time Paul means (m1).

records.source: οἴδατε δὲ ὅτι δι’ ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς εὐηγγελισάμην ὑμῖν τὸ πρότερον, καὶ τὸν πειρασμὸν ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου οὐκ ἐξουθενήσατε οὐδὲ ἐξεπτύσατε, ἀλλὰ ὡς ἄγγελον θεοῦ ἐδέξασθέ με, ὡς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν.
records.gloss: And you know that because of weakness of the flesh I proclaimed the gospel to you the former [time], \v 14 and the trial of you in the flesh of me not you despised nor you spat out, but as an angel of God you received me, as Christ Jesus.
pieces: You know that I preached the gospel to you the first time because of a weakness of the flesh.

And though my flesh was a trial to you, you did not scorn me or spit in disgust. No, you received me like an angel of God, like {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}.

L.13: And you know that because of a weakness of the flesh I preached the gospel to you the first time,
L.14: and your trial in my flesh you did not despise or spit out, but you received me as an angel of God, as {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} Jesus.

R.13: You know that the first time I told you the good news, it was because I was sick.
R.14: My illness was hard for you to bear, but you did not look down on me or turn away from me in disgust. You treated me like an angel sent from God, even like {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} Jesus {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}.

decisions.choice: because of an illness in his body
alternatives: in weakness, with "weakness" meaning humble circumstances
decisions.reason: With δι and the accusative, Paul gives the reason he preached there: some illness kept him among the Galatians or brought him to them. "Weakness of the flesh" is bodily weakness. What the illness was cannot be known; verse 15 may hint that it affected his eyes.

decisions.choice: the first time
decisions.reason: τὸ πρότερον can mean "the first of two times" or simply "earlier". If the first, Paul had visited them twice before writing.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "your trial"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "my trial" or have no pronoun. The SBLGNT follows early manuscripts that read "your": Paul's illness put the Galatians to the test, tempting them to reject him. The harder reading is more likely to have been changed by copyists than created.

decisions.choice: spit out: a gesture of disgust or of warding off evil
decisions.reason: ἐκπτύω means to spit out. People spat at the sight of the sick and the afflicted to show disgust or to ward off evil and sickness. The Galatians did no such thing.

decisions.choice: an angel of God
decisions.reason: ἄγγελος can mean a human messenger or an angel. Here it rises to "as Christ Jesus", so Paul means they received him as they would a heavenly messenger, and more than that, as Christ himself.

decisions.choice: I was sick; my illness
decisions.reason: Here "flesh" is the body, and its weakness an illness (m1); Readable says so plainly. Literal and Balanced keep "flesh".

decisions.choice: like ... himself
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "like" for the comparison. "Himself" marks the climax, from an angel to Christ.

records.source: ποῦ οὖν ὁ μακαρισμὸς ὑμῶν;
records.gloss: Where then the blessedness of you?
pieces: What has become, then, of the way you once counted yourselves blessed?

R.15: Back then you said how blessed you were. What has happened to that?

decisions.choice: your counting yourselves blessed
alternatives: the blessing you spoke over me
decisions.reason: μακαρισμός is the act of calling someone blessed or fortunate. Most likely the Galatians counted themselves blessed to have Paul and his gospel; it could also be their blessing of him. Either way, that warmth is gone.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "where"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "what", which turns the question into a reminder of how happy they were. The SBLGNT reads "where", which asks where that happiness has gone. The point is close.

decisions.choice: the way you once counted yourselves blessed (B); back then you said how blessed you were (R)
decisions.reason: "Your blessedness" says little in English; Balanced and Readable say what it was (m1).

records.source: μαρτυρῶ γὰρ ὑμῖν ὅτι εἰ δυνατὸν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὑμῶν ἐξορύξαντες ἐδώκατέ μοι.
records.gloss: For I testify to you that if possible, the eyes of you having dug out you gave [them] to me.
pieces: I can vouch for you: you would have gouged out your own eyes and handed them to me if that had been possible.

L.15: For I testify to you that, if [it had been] possible, you would have dug out your eyes [and] given [them] to me.

R.15: I can tell you for sure that you would have pulled out your own eyes and given them to me if you could.

decisions.choice: you would have torn out your eyes for me: you would have given me anything
decisions.reason: The eyes stood for what is most precious (Deuteronomy 32:10; Psalm 17:8). Giving them away is a picture of total devotion.

decisions.choice: perhaps a hint that Paul's illness affected his eyes
decisions.reason: Some take the picture literally, as if the Galatians wished to give Paul healthy eyes in place of his own; 6:11, where he writes in large letters, has been read the same way. The saying works just as well as a general picture of devotion, so this cannot be settled.

records.source: ὥστε ἐχθρὸς ὑμῶν γέγονα ἀληθεύων ὑμῖν;
records.gloss: So enemy of you have I become speaking truth to you?
pieces: So is it the truth I tell you that has made me your enemy?

L.16: So have I become your enemy, telling you [the] truth?

R.16: So now have I become your enemy, just because I tell you the truth?

decisions.choice: a question: have I become your enemy?
alternatives: a statement: so I have become your enemy
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates it as a question, a sad and pointed one. Read as a statement, it is the bitter conclusion of verses 13-15.

decisions.choice: by telling you the truth
decisions.reason: The participle gives the cause: what has turned them against Paul is the truth he tells them, whether in this letter or on an earlier visit.

records.source: ζηλοῦσιν ὑμᾶς οὐ καλῶς, ἀλλὰ ἐκκλεῖσαι ὑμᾶς θέλουσιν, ἵνα αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦτε.
records.gloss: They are zealous for you not well, but to shut out you they want, so that them you may be zealous for.
pieces: These people pay you eager attention, but their motives are not good. They want to shut you out, so that you will pay eager attention to them.

L.17: They are zealous for you, not rightly, but they want to shut you out, so that you may be zealous for them.

R.17: Those teachers are trying hard to win you over, but what they want is not good. They want to shut you out, so that you will try hard to please them instead.

decisions.choice: they: those who are unsettling the Galatians
decisions.reason: Paul does not name them; they are the people of 1:7 and 5:10 who want the Galatians circumcised.

decisions.choice: court: eagerly seek someone's devotion
decisions.reason: ζηλόω can mean to be zealous, to be jealous, or to seek someone eagerly, as a suitor does (2 Corinthians 11:2). Paul uses it twice: they court the Galatians so that the Galatians will court them.

decisions.choice: shut you out: from Paul, and from the freedom of the gospel
alternatives: shut you out from God's people unless you are circumcised
decisions.reason: Paul does not say from what. It may be from him and his teaching, so that they will depend on the new teachers, or from the people of God unless they keep the law. Both readings make the teachers' aim self-serving.

decisions.choice: are zealous for (L); pay eager attention (B)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the repeated verb; Balanced gives its sense here (m2).

decisions.choice: Those teachers
decisions.reason: Readable names who "they" are (m1).

records.source: καλὸν δὲ ζηλοῦσθαι ἐν καλῷ πάντοτε, καὶ μὴ μόνον ἐν τῷ παρεῖναί με πρὸς ὑμᾶς, τέκνα μου, οὓς πάλιν ὠδίνω μέχρις οὗ μορφωθῇ Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν·
records.gloss: And good to be courted in good always, and not only in the being present me with you, \v 19 children of me, whom again I am in labor until is formed Christ in you;
pieces: It is always good to be sought after for a good purpose, and not only when I am there with you.
My children, I am suffering birth pains over you a second time, and I will until {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is formed in you.

L.18: Now it is good to be sought eagerly in a good [thing] always, and not only when I am present with you,
L.19: my children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} is formed in you.

R.18: It is good for people to care about you, if their purpose is good. That should be true all the time, not only when I am there with you.
R.19: My children, I am going through pain for you again, like a mother giving birth. I will keep on until {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} takes shape in your lives.

decisions.choice: to be sought after: the Galatians are the ones courted
alternatives: to be zealous yourselves for what is good
decisions.reason: ζηλοῦσθαι is most naturally passive here, taking up verse 17: it is good for the Galatians to be courted, as long as it is for a good purpose, whether Paul is with them or not. It could also be read as "to be zealous", urging the Galatians themselves.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "children"
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts have the diminutive "little children", Paul's word nowhere else but common in John's letters. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: I am in labor for you again: Paul as a mother
decisions.reason: ὠδίνω means to suffer the pains of childbirth. Paul pictures himself as a mother who has given birth to these believers once, through his first preaching, and must go through it a second time.

decisions.choice: until Christ is formed in you: until their life takes Christ's shape
alternatives: until Christ is born in you
decisions.reason: μορφόω means to give form or shape. The picture moves from Paul giving birth to Christ taking shape in them, both in each believer and in the church as a whole. It echoes 2:20, "Christ lives in me".

decisions.choice: like a mother giving birth
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that Paul is comparing himself to a mother (m3).

decisions.choice: takes shape in your lives
decisions.reason: Readable says where the shaping happens: in how they live (m4).

records.source: ἤθελον δὲ παρεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἄρτι, καὶ ἀλλάξαι τὴν φωνήν μου, ὅτι ἀποροῦμαι ἐν ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: And I was wishing to be present with you now and to change the voice of me, because I am at a loss in you.
pieces: I would like to be there with you now and speak in another tone, for I do not know what to make of you.

L.20: And I could wish to be present with you now and to change my voice, because I am at a loss about you.

R.20: I wish I could be with you right now. Then I could speak to you in a different way. I just do not know what to do about you.

decisions.choice: I wish: a wish that cannot be carried out now
decisions.reason: The past tense ἤθελον here expresses a present wish Paul cannot fulfill: he would like to be there, but he is not.

decisions.choice: change my tone: speak to them differently than a letter allows
alternatives: speak more gently than this letter does
decisions.reason: Face to face Paul could suit his words to what he found, perhaps more gently than the sharp words of this letter. Which change he has in mind is not said.

decisions.choice: I am at a loss: I do not know what to make of you or what to do
decisions.reason: ἀπορέω means to be perplexed, without a way forward.

decisions.choice: I would like (B); I wish (R)
decisions.reason: English expresses this kind of wish with a present tense (m1).

records.source: Λέγετέ μοι, οἱ ὑπὸ νόμον θέλοντες εἶναι, τὸν νόμον οὐκ ἀκούετε;
records.gloss: Tell me, those under law wishing to be, the law not do you hear?
pieces: You who want to be under the law, tell me: do you not hear what the law says?

L.21: Tell me, you who want to be under [the] law, do you not listen to the law?

R.21: You want to live under the law. Then tell me, do you not listen to what the law itself says?

decisions.choice: the law the second time: the books of Moses as Scripture, here the story in Genesis
alternatives: the same sense both times: the commandments
decisions.reason: Paul uses νόμον twice with two senses. "Under law" is the law of Moses as a way of life that rules a person (3:23, 4:4-5). "The law" they should listen to is the written Law, the five books of Moses, which include the story of Abraham's sons that he is about to tell (Genesis 16-21). His point is that the law itself speaks against what they want.

decisions.choice: listen to: hear with understanding and take to heart
decisions.reason: ἀκούω can mean simply to hear a text read aloud, as the law was read in the synagogues, but here Paul asks whether they really hear what it says. The question expects the answer that they do not.

decisions.choice: those who want to be under law: people still deciding, drawn toward it
decisions.reason: The present participle θέλοντες describes what the Galatians wish for now. They have not yet taken on the law in full; Paul is warning them before they do (compare 4:9-10, 5:2-3).

decisions.choice: You want to live under the law. Then tell me ... what the law itself says
alternatives: Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?
decisions.reason: Readable splits the question in two and adds "itself" to show the turn in Paul's argument: the law they want points away from the law (m1).

records.heading: Hagar and Sarah: two covenants

records.source: γέγραπται γὰρ ὅτι Ἀβραὰμ δύο υἱοὺς ἔσχεν, ἕνα ἐκ τῆς παιδίσκης καὶ ἕνα ἐκ τῆς ἐλευθέρας·
records.gloss: It has been written for that Abraham two sons had, one from the slave woman and one from the free.
pieces: Scripture says that Abraham had two sons: one was the son of the slave woman, the other the son of the free woman.

L.22: For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one from the slave woman and one from the free [woman].

R.22: The Scriptures say that Abraham had two sons. One son's mother was a slave woman. The other son's mother was a free woman.

decisions.choice: a summary of Genesis 16-21: Ishmael born to Hagar, Isaac born to Sarah
decisions.reason: "It is written" (γέγραπται) introduces not a quotation but a summary of the Genesis story: Hagar, Sarah's Egyptian slave, bore Ishmael to Abraham (Genesis 16:1-4, 15), and Sarah bore Isaac (Genesis 21:1-3). Abraham had other sons later (Genesis 25:1-2); Paul speaks only of these two.

decisions.choice: slave woman: a female slave, owned by her mistress
decisions.reason: παιδίσκη can mean a young girl, but in Paul's day it most often meant a female slave. Genesis 16:1 says Hagar was Sarah's slave, and Paul builds his whole contrast on slave and free (4:23-31, 5:1).

decisions.choice: slave woman
decisions.reason: "Slave woman" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free: the contrast with "free" carries the passage, and "servant" would hide that Hagar was owned. Older words such as "bondwoman" or "handmaid" are no longer plain English.

decisions.choice: free [woman] (L); free woman (B, R)
decisions.reason: ἐλευθέρας is a feminine adjective used as a noun, "the free one", meaning Sarah. English needs "woman".

decisions.choice: Scripture says
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the sense of the set formula "it has been written": this is what Scripture records.

records.source: ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἐκ τῆς παιδίσκης κατὰ σάρκα γεγέννηται, ὁ δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἐλευθέρας δι’ ἐπαγγελίας.
records.gloss: But the [one] indeed from the slave woman according to flesh has been born, the [one] but from the free through promise.
pieces: The slave woman's son was born according to the flesh, but the free woman's son was born through the promise.

L.23: But the [one] from the slave woman was born according to [the] flesh, and the [one] from the free [woman] through [the] promise.

R.23: The slave woman's son was born in the ordinary way, through a plan people made. But the free woman's son was born because of what God had promised.

decisions.choice: according to the flesh: by ordinary human means, as people arranged it
decisions.reason: Here σάρξ is not the sinful self of 5:13-24 but natural human birth. Ishmael was born in the normal course of things, by Sarah's own plan to have a child through Hagar (Genesis 16:2). Isaac was born when Sarah was past bearing, only because God had promised it (Genesis 17:16-19, 18:10-14, 21:1-2).

decisions.choice: through the promise: God's promise to Abraham of a son by Sarah
decisions.reason: ἐπαγγελία links back to 3:16-18, where the inheritance comes by promise and not by law. Isaac's birth is the first proof that God gives what he promises, and does it himself.

decisions.choice: has been born: the birth stands written in Scripture, and its result goes on
decisions.reason: The perfect tense γεγέννηται presents the birth as a fact on record with lasting effect: the two kinds of children still exist (4:28-29).

decisions.choice: the slave woman's son ... the free woman's son
decisions.reason: The Greek has only the article (ὁ), "the one"; the sons of verse 22 are meant.

decisions.choice: in the ordinary way, through a plan people made ... because of what God had promised
alternatives: according to the flesh ... through the promise
decisions.reason: Readable explains the two phrases from the Genesis story (m1, m2). "Flesh" alone would make a young reader think of the body or of sin.

decisions.choice: slave woman
decisions.reason: "Slave woman" at every level, as in 4:22: the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free.

records.source: ἅτινά ἐστιν ἀλληγορούμενα· αὗται γάρ εἰσιν δύο διαθῆκαι, μία μὲν ἀπὸ ὄρους Σινᾶ, εἰς δουλείαν γεννῶσα, ἥτις ἐστὶν Ἁγάρ, τὸ δὲ Ἁγὰρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ, συστοιχεῖ δὲ τῇ νῦν Ἰερουσαλήμ, δουλεύει γὰρ μετὰ τῶν τέκνων αὐτῆς·
records.gloss: Which things are being allegorized; these for are two covenants, one indeed from mount Sinai, unto slavery bearing, which is Hagar. \v 25 The now Hagar Sinai mountain is in the Arabia, corresponds now to the now Jerusalem, is enslaved for with the children of her.
pieces: These things can be read as an allegory. The two women are two covenants. One comes from Mount Sinai and bears children who will be slaves; this is Hagar.
Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she matches the Jerusalem of the present time, since she is in slavery together with her children.

L.24: These things are spoken allegorically, for these [women] are two covenants: one from Mount Sinai, bearing [children] into slavery, which is Hagar.
L.25: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.

R.24: This story is also a picture of something else. The two women stand for two covenants. One covenant came from Mount Sinai, and the children born under it are slaves. That covenant is Hagar.
R.25: Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia. She is like the city of Jerusalem today, because Jerusalem and her people are living as slaves.

decisions.choice: spoken allegorically: the story also says something beyond itself
alternatives: the story is only a parable and did not happen
a pattern in history (typology) rather than an allegory
decisions.reason: ἀλληγορέω means to speak or read a text so that it carries a further meaning. Paul does not deny that the events happened; he has just told them as history (4:22-23). He reads the two mothers and their sons as pictures of two covenants and the people who belong to each.

decisions.choice: these are two covenants: the two women stand for two covenants
decisions.reason: αὗται is feminine and points back to the two women. "Are" means "represent", as Hagar "is" Mount Sinai in verse 25.

decisions.choice: one ...: the second covenant is never named
decisions.reason: μία μὲν ("one on the one hand") leads the reader to expect "the other ...", but Paul never states it. He moves to the Jerusalem above in verse 26, which takes the place of the second covenant and of Sarah, who is not named either. The covenant of promise made with Abraham (3:15-18) is meant.

decisions.choice: bearing children into slavery: those born under the Sinai covenant are slaves under the law
decisions.reason: As Hagar, a slave, bore a son who was a slave, so the covenant given at Sinai produces people who live under the law as slaves. Paul has said this already in 4:1-3 and 4:8-9 and says it again in 5:1.

decisions.choice: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai: the SBLGNT reading, with Hagar's name
alternatives: For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ here. Some have "for" in place of "now", and some leave out the name Hagar, giving "for Sinai is a mountain in Arabia", a plain remark of geography. The SBLGNT keeps the name. The neuter article before Hagar's name treats it as a word or a figure: "this Hagar" of the allegory. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Arabia: the lands south and east of Judea, outside the land of promise
decisions.reason: In Paul's day "Arabia" covered the desert lands from the Sinai peninsula to beyond the Jordan, where Paul himself went after his conversion (1:17). Hagar's son Ishmael and his descendants lived in this region (Genesis 21:21, 25:12-18). So the mountain where the law was given lies in Hagar's country, outside the land promised to Abraham.

decisions.choice: corresponds to: stands in the same column as the present Jerusalem
decisions.reason: συστοιχέω means to stand in the same row or line, like soldiers in a file. Paul sets out two columns: Hagar, Sinai, slavery and the present Jerusalem in one; Sarah, promise, freedom and the Jerusalem above in the other (4:26). "The present Jerusalem" is the city as the center of life under the law, from which the teachers pressing circumcision drew their authority (compare 2:12).

decisions.choice: in slavery with her children: Jerusalem and its people are slaves under the law
decisions.reason: A city is often pictured as a mother and its people as her children. The slavery is the one Paul has been describing, under the law (4:3, 4:9, 5:1). Jerusalem was also under Roman rule, but that is not Paul's point.

decisions.choice: these [women] (L); The two women (B, R)
decisions.reason: English needs a noun for the feminine pronoun (m2).

decisions.choice: stands for
decisions.reason: The verb "is" here means "represents" (m2). Balanced and Readable say so; Literal keeps "is".

decisions.choice: This story is also a picture of something else ... Jerusalem and her people are living as slaves
alternatives: These things are an allegory ... she is in slavery with her children
decisions.reason: Readable avoids the word "allegory" and says that the story is also a picture (m1). It names "her children" as Jerusalem's people (m8).

decisions.choice: slaves / in slavery
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it where slavery under the law or the elemental forces is set against freedom (Galatians 4–5). Hagar and Sinai stand in the column of slavery against Sarah and freedom (m4, m7, m8).

records.source: ἡ δὲ ἄνω Ἰερουσαλὴμ ἐλευθέρα ἐστίν, ἥτις ἐστὶν μήτηρ ἡμῶν·
records.gloss: The but above Jerusalem free is, who is mother of us.
pieces: The Jerusalem above, however, is free, and it is she who is our mother.

L.26: But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother.

R.26: But there is another Jerusalem, God's city in heaven. She is free, and she is our mother.

decisions.choice: the Jerusalem above: God's heavenly city, where he reigns and his people belong
decisions.reason: ἄνω ("above") is set against "present" (νῦν) in verse 25. Paul contrasts not two places on earth but the city of this age with the city of God, which belongs to the age to come and is already the home of believers. Compare Philippians 3:20, Hebrews 12:22 and Revelation 21:2.

decisions.choice: who is our mother: the free woman of the allegory, standing where Sarah stands
decisions.reason: Paul does not name Sarah, but the Jerusalem above takes her place as the free woman whose children are free (4:31). "Our" includes Paul, a Jew, and the Galatians, Gentiles: all who believe are her children.

decisions.choice: our mother: the SBLGNT reading
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add a word meaning "all", giving "the mother of us all", the reading of the King James Version. The earliest manuscripts do not have it. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: there is another Jerusalem, God's city in heaven
decisions.reason: "The Jerusalem above" would puzzle a young reader; Readable says what it is (m1).

records.source: γέγραπται γάρ· Εὐφράνθητι, στεῖρα ἡ οὐ τίκτουσα, ῥῆξον καὶ βόησον, ἡ οὐκ ὠδίνουσα· ὅτι πολλὰ τὰ τέκνα τῆς ἐρήμου μᾶλλον ἢ τῆς ἐχούσης τὸν ἄνδρα.
records.gloss: It has been written for: Rejoice, barren [one] the not bearing, break forth and shout, the not travailing; because many the children of the desolate more than of the [one] having the husband.
pieces: For it is written: "Be glad, barren woman, you who have borne no child; break into a shout, you who have never been in labor. For the woman left alone has many children, more than the woman who has a husband."

L.27: For it is written: "Rejoice, barren [woman] who does not bear; break out and shout, you who are not in labor; for many [are] the children of the desolate [woman], more than of her who has the husband."

R.27: The Scriptures say, "Be glad, you woman who could never have children! You never felt the pains of giving birth, but now break out and shout for joy! The woman who was left alone has more children than the woman who has a husband."

decisions.choice: a quotation of Isaiah 54:1, word for word as in the Greek Old Testament
decisions.reason: Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem after the exile as a barren woman, abandoned and childless, and promises that her children will be more than she can count. Paul joins the barren woman to Sarah, who was barren (Genesis 11:30) and became the mother of the promised son, and so to the Jerusalem above (4:26). The many children are those who now believe, Gentiles among them.

decisions.choice: the desolate woman: a woman left alone, deserted
decisions.reason: ἔρημος can mean a desert, but here it describes a woman without husband or children, as Jerusalem was left desolate in exile (Isaiah 54:4-6).

decisions.choice: the woman who has the husband: in Paul's reading, Hagar
alternatives: only Isaiah's picture, with no application to Hagar
decisions.reason: In Isaiah the married woman stands for a city with all its people. Paul seems to apply her to Hagar, whom Sarah gave to Abraham as a wife (Genesis 16:3) and who bore him a son, while Sarah stayed barren. He does not say this outright, so the link is likely rather than certain.

decisions.choice: break forth and shout: burst out in a cry of joy
decisions.reason: ῥήγνυμι means to break or burst; with "shout" it pictures someone bursting into a joyful cry, as in Isaiah 49:13, where the hills break into song.

decisions.choice: the woman left alone has many children, more than (B); has more children than (R)
alternatives: more are the children of the desolate
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb; Balanced and Readable supply "has" to make a sentence. "Left alone" is plainer than "desolate" (m2).

decisions.choice: but now break out and shout for joy
decisions.reason: Readable adds "for joy" (m4) and "now" to mark the change from her past grief.

records.source: ὑμεῖς δέ, ἀδελφοί, κατὰ Ἰσαὰκ ἐπαγγελίας τέκνα ἐστέ·
records.gloss: You now, brothers, like Isaac of promise children are.
pieces: And you, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, are children of the promise, as Isaac was.

L.28: But you, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, are children of promise like Isaac.

R.28: And you, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, are like Isaac. You are children born because of what God promised.

decisions.choice: like Isaac: after the pattern of Isaac
decisions.reason: κατὰ with a name means "in the manner of". The Galatians were not born of Sarah, but like Isaac they owe their place in Abraham's family to God's promise, not to human descent or effort (3:29).

decisions.choice: children of promise: children whose life in God's family comes from his promise
decisions.reason: Isaac was born because God promised him (4:23). In the same way the Galatians, Gentiles who believed, became Abraham's children through the promise given to Abraham and fulfilled in Christ (3:14, 3:29).

decisions.choice: you are: the SBLGNT reading
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts read "we are" here, matching "our mother" in verse 26 and "we are" in verse 31. The SBLGNT reads "you are", and the change to "we" is easier to explain as a scribe's smoothing than the reverse. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is writing to the whole church in Galatia, women and men, and has just said that in Christ there is neither male nor female (3:28). "Brothers" stays available as the traditional form.

decisions.choice: children born because of what God promised
decisions.reason: Readable explains "children of promise" from verse 23 (m2).

records.source: ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ τότε ὁ κατὰ σάρκα γεννηθεὶς ἐδίωκε τὸν κατὰ πνεῦμα, οὕτως καὶ νῦν.
records.gloss: But just as then the [one] according to flesh having been born was persecuting the [one] according to Spirit, so also now.
pieces: In those days the son born according to the flesh persecuted the son born according to the Spirit, and it is the same now.

L.29: But just as at that time the [one] born according to [the] flesh persecuted the [one born] according to [the] Spirit, so [it is] also now.

R.29: But back then, the son born in the ordinary human way mistreated the son born by the power of the Spirit. The same thing is happening now.

decisions.choice: persecuted: Paul's reading of Genesis 21:9, where Sarah sees Ishmael with Isaac
alternatives: a stronger word than Genesis supports
decisions.reason: Genesis 21:9 says Sarah saw Hagar's son "laughing" or "playing", a Hebrew word that can also mean mocking; the Greek Old Testament adds that he was playing with Isaac. Genesis does not use a word for persecution. Paul reads the scene as hostility from the older son to the younger, which is how it was often understood among Jews of his time.

decisions.choice: according to the Spirit: born by the power of God's Spirit, who fulfilled the promise
decisions.reason: πνεῦμα here is the Spirit of God. Verse 23 said Isaac was born "through the promise"; now Paul says "according to the Spirit", because it was God's power that gave a child to a barren woman. The Galatians also began with the Spirit (3:2-5).

decisions.choice: born according to the flesh: by ordinary human means, as in verse 23
decisions.reason: σάρξ has the same sense as in verse 23: natural birth by human arrangement. Applied to Paul's day, it describes those who rely on what is done in the body, circumcision (6:12-13).

decisions.choice: so also now: those who insist on the law are pressing hard on those who live by the promise
decisions.reason: Paul means the pressure on the Galatians and on himself from those who demand circumcision (5:11, 6:12). He does not name them here.

decisions.choice: the son born ... the son born
decisions.reason: The Greek has only articles, "the one"; the two sons of verse 22 are meant.

decisions.choice: mistreated
decisions.reason: Genesis tells of a quarrel at home, not of a persecution in the later sense (m1); "mistreated" is plain and fits both scenes. Literal and Balanced keep "persecuted".

records.source: ἀλλὰ τί λέγει ἡ γραφή;
records.gloss: But what says the Scripture?
pieces: But what does Scripture say?

L.30: But what does the Scripture say?

R.30: But what do the Scriptures say?

decisions.choice: the Scripture: the particular passage about to be quoted, Genesis 21:10
decisions.reason: γραφή in the singular often means one passage of Scripture. Paul makes it speak, as in 3:8 and 3:22: what it says is what God says.

decisions.choice: the Scriptures
decisions.reason: Readable uses the plural, the ordinary way to speak of the Bible, as in verse 22.

records.source: Ἔκβαλε τὴν παιδίσκην καὶ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῆς, οὐ γὰρ μὴ κληρονομήσει ὁ υἱὸς τῆς παιδίσκης μετὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἐλευθέρας.
records.gloss: Cast out the slave woman and the son of her, for no not will inherit the son of the slave woman with the son of the free.
pieces: "Send away the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman's son will never share the inheritance with the free woman's son."

L.30: "Drive out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman will by no means inherit with the son of the free [woman]."

R.30: "Send the slave woman and her son away. The slave woman's son will never share the inheritance with the free woman's son."

decisions.choice: a quotation of Genesis 21:10, Sarah's words to Abraham
decisions.reason: In Genesis Sarah says the slave woman's son will not inherit "with my son Isaac". Paul writes "with the son of the free woman" to fit his argument. In Genesis 21:12 God tells Abraham to do what Sarah says, so Paul can quote it as what Scripture says.

decisions.choice: will never inherit: the strongest possible denial
decisions.reason: οὐ μὴ with a future verb rules something out completely.

decisions.choice: inherit: receive what was promised to Abraham's heirs
decisions.reason: κληρονομέω takes up Paul's theme of the inheritance, which comes by promise and not by law (3:18, 3:29, 4:1-7). Only the children of the free woman are heirs.

decisions.choice: drive out: Scripture rules that the way of the law and the way of promise cannot share the inheritance
alternatives: a direct command to expel the teachers
a statement of God's verdict, not a command to the church
decisions.reason: Paul may be telling the Galatians to send away the teachers who demand circumcision, or he may be stating God's verdict that those who rely on the law have no share with the children of promise. Either way the slave woman and her son stand for life under the law (4:24-25).

decisions.choice: Drive out (L); Send away (B, R)
decisions.reason: ἐκβάλλω is a strong word, used of driving out or expelling. Literal keeps that force; Balanced and Readable use "send away", which is what Abraham did in Genesis 21:14.

decisions.choice: slave woman
decisions.reason: "Slave woman" at every level, as in 4:22: the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free.

records.source: διό, ἀδελφοί, οὐκ ἐσμὲν παιδίσκης τέκνα ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐλευθέρας.
records.gloss: Therefore, brothers, not we are of slave woman children but of the free.
pieces: So then, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, we are children not of a slave woman but of the free woman.

L.31: Therefore, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, we are not children of a slave woman but of the free [woman].

R.31: So, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, we are not the children of a slave woman. We are the children of the free woman.

decisions.choice: a slave woman ... the free woman: the article marks the one free woman
decisions.reason: παιδίσκης has no article, "a slave woman", while τῆς ἐλευθέρας has one, "the free woman". Paul may mean that there is only one free mother, the Jerusalem above (4:26), while slavery can come in more than one form. The difference may also be only a matter of style.

decisions.choice: Therefore: the conclusion of 4:21-30, which also leads into 5:1
decisions.reason: διό draws the conclusion of the allegory. The first sentence of chapter 5 then says what follows from being free; some readers take 4:31 and 5:1 as one thought.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is writing to the whole church in Galatia, women and men, and has just said that in Christ there is neither male nor female (3:28). "Brothers" stays available as the traditional form.

decisions.choice: slave woman
decisions.reason: "Slave woman" at every level, as in 4:22: the style guide keeps it where slave is set against free.
